title: Library system LLD
idea: A small LLD case study turns a library's rules into a handful of classes: nouns become types, verbs become methods, and changing rules sit behind interfaces.
points: Start from use cases: lend a copy, return it, charge a late fine.
Separate `Book`, the title, from `BookCopy`, the physical item you lend.
A `Loan` record links one copy to one member with a due day.
Inject the `FinePolicy`, because fine rules change more often than lending does.

steps.caption: Requirement: a title can have several copies. So `Book` and `BookCopy` are separate classes.
`Library` owns the copies and is the one entry point for lending.
Lending creates a `Loan`: which copy, which member, due on which day.
Members have a loan limit. `lend` counts open loans before it hands out a copy.
Fine rules vary, so `Library` depends on the `FinePolicy` interface, injected through its constructor.
`PerDayFine` is one rule. A capped or student rule would be a new class, not an edit.

code.caption: Mermaid source for the class diagram. Draw this before you write any code.

walk.text: `FinePolicy` is marked `<<interface>>`: a role, not a concrete class.
Each class lists only the fields the use cases need.
`Library` exposes what the use cases need: add a copy, lend, give back.
Arrows show has-a links; `o--` marks a collection the library holds.
The library depends on the interface; `..|>` means implements.

code.title: The design, running
code.caption: One copy, two members: the second must wait, and a late return earns a fine.

walk.text: Value objects are `record`s: small, immutable and compared by value.
The fine rule sits behind an interface; returning a book on time costs nothing.
`Library` keeps copies and open loans private; the policy arrives by constructor.
Rule one: refuse a member who is already at the loan limit.
Rule two: find a copy of the title that is not out, or refuse.
Returning closes the loan and asks the policy for the fine.
The demo walks the main use cases, including a refusal.

pitfalls: Do not merge `Book` and `BookCopy`; you cannot then lend two copies of one title.
Avoid one god class doing search, lending, fines and notices; split by responsibility.
Clarify requirements first: limits, due periods and fine rules shape the classes.

quiz.q: Using the classes above, what does this print?
quiz.why: The loan is due on day 14. Returning on day 12 gives -2 days late, and `Math.max(0, daysLate)` turns that into 0.

takeaway: Find nouns and rules, give each a class, and inject what varies.

starters: How would I add reservations when no copy is free?
Where should search by author or title live in this design?
How would this design change for an interview follow-up on concurrency?
